unit.unitOverview: Tell the story of something that happened, so nobody has to ask what order it came in. Set a scene that is already running, let one event land in it, and mark what had gone wrong before any of it. Say how long you have been doing something, not just how much you have done. Then join two events into one sentence without repeating yourself.
unit.learningPath:
The lesson: listen first, then read it back.
Words: five groups, 29 words. Listen and say each one.

Reading: an account of an incident, a language guide and an incident report.
Questions: 10 about the three texts.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, listen back.
Writing: four tasks, each with a model.
Practice and the check: 7 exercises, then 12 questions.

visual.lectureScript:
This unit is about telling somebody what happened, and it is more useful than it sounds.
An account of an incident is read by people who were not there, sometimes months later, sometimes in a dispute.
What makes one good is not the vocabulary. It is that the order of events is beyond argument.

There is one genuinely new form here, and it is the first card.
The present perfect continuous. Have been, plus the -ing form.
I have been working here for six years. She has been waiting since nine.
You already have the present perfect, from seven cards below this one and from Unit 3.
What this adds is the activity itself rather than the result.
Somebody comes in soaked, and you say it has been raining. Not it has rained.
It has rained is a fact. It has been raining explains what is in front of you.
The usual warning applies. State verbs refuse it. I have known her for years, never I have been knowing her.

The second card is the choice, and there is one test that settles most of it.
Is there a number?
I have written three reports. That is a number, so it has to be the simple. You cannot count an activity that has not finished.
I have been writing reports all day. That is a stretch, so it is the continuous.
And there is a second pair worth having.
I have painted the door means the door is painted. The job is done.
I have been painting the door means look at the state of me.
Simple for the result and the count. Continuous for the activity and the stretch.

The third card is how a narrative actually opens, and it uses something you already have in a new way.
Unit 1 used the past continuous for a long stretch of your life. Here it is much shorter and much more useful.
It was getting dark, the yard was emptying, and nobody was speaking.
Three clauses, all continuous, and nothing has happened yet. That is the point. It is the scene, still running.
Then one thing lands, in the past simple. A trolley crashed into the racking.
And anything that had already gone wrong before any of it goes into the past perfect. The brake had not been set.
Three layers, three tenses. Before, background, event.
If you write the whole thing in the past simple, a reader cannot tell which part was the event.
And if you write the whole thing in the continuous, nothing ever happens.

The fourth card completes something Unit 8 started.
Unit 8 gave you Having finished, which marks something earlier, and Being told, which marks something done to you.
The third kind is the plain -ing clause, and it marks something happening at the same moment.
Walking into the yard, I saw that the gate was open.
It can also come after the main clause, where it adds a result very economically.
The trolley hit the racking, bringing two shelves down with it.
And the rule has not changed. The clause and the main clause must share a subject.
Walking into the yard, the gate was standing open says the gate was walking.

The last card is a small thing that produces a very common error.
Three frames in English refuse the past simple, whatever the time involved.
After a superlative. That is the worst damage I have ever seen. Not I ever saw.
After the first time, the second time, the only time. This is the first time I have given a statement.
And after phrases like the one thing nobody has explained.
There is a reason, and knowing it makes the rule stick. All three of those measure something up to the moment you are standing in.
Ever seen means across my whole life, ending now. The past simple closes a period off, and these frames will not be closed.
There is a neat consequence. Move the frame into the past and the verb moves with it.
It was the first time I had given a statement.
So the rule is not really about the perfect. It is about how far the frame reaches.
Start with the words. Say each one aloud before you move on.

readings.title: Four Minutes in the Yard
readings.setting: A distribution depot, told two days afterwards
readings.passageScript:
It was getting dark, the yard was emptying, and nobody was speaking.
I have worked there for eleven years and I had never seen it that quiet at five o'clock.
I was checking the racking against the list when a trolley crashed into the end of it.
Walking round the corner, I saw that two shelves had come down and the top one was still moving.
Somebody behind me gasped. Nobody panicked, which surprised me afterwards.
I froze for about a second, and then three of us rushed towards it simultaneously.
The whole incident took four minutes. The aftermath took two days.
The trolley had been left on the slope, which is not allowed, and the brake had not been set.
Nobody had checked it beforehand because the yard team had been working short all week.
That is the worst damage I have ever seen there, and it was nobody's single fault.
This is the first time I have given a written statement about anything.
What I have learned from it is that the sequence matters more than the detail.
I have been trying to write down exactly what happened first, and two days later I still cannot be sure.

readings.title: Three Things That Refuse the Past Simple
readings.setting: A page from a language guide
readings.passageScript:
Most tense choices in English are decided by meaning. Three are decided by the words around them.
After a superlative, English uses the present perfect.
That is the worst damage I have ever seen. Not the worst damage I ever saw.
After the first time, the second time or the only time, it does the same.
This is the first time I have given a statement. Not the first time I gave one.
And after phrases like the one thing or the only thing, again the same.
There is a reason, and it is worth knowing because it makes the rule stick.
All three of those frames measure something up to the present moment.
Ever seen means across my whole life, ending now.
The first time means counted up to today.
The past simple closes a period off and puts a wall at the end of it, and these frames will not be closed.
There is a useful consequence. If you move the frame into the past, the verb moves with it.
It WAS the first time I HAD given a statement.
So the rule is not about the perfect. It is about the frame reaching the moment you are standing in.

readings.passageScript:
INCIDENT REPORT
Reference: IN-4471        Location: Yard, north end        Date: 14 November, 17:04
Reported by: A. Whitmore, racking check        Form completed: 16 November

1. Conditions at the time
Light was failing. The yard was emptying at the end of the shift.
Two of the four floodlights were out and had been reported on 7 November.

2. Sequence
17:04  A trolley ran down the slope and struck the end bay of the racking.
17:04  Two shelves came down. The upper shelf was still moving when I reached it.
17:05  Three staff attended. The area was cleared.
17:08  The yard supervisor was informed and the bay was sealed.

3. Contributing factors
The trolley had been left on the slope, contrary to procedure.
Its brake had not been set. The brake has since been found to be faulty.
The yard team had been working one short since 10 November.

4. Injuries
None. Nobody was standing in the bay at the time.

5. Action
The bay remains sealed. A replacement trolley has been issued.
This is the third time a trolley has been found unbraked this quarter.

grammar.title: I have been working here: the form that shows the effort
grammar.explanation:
This form is new. Unit 3 gave you the present perfect, and seven cards below
that gave you its pieces. None of them could show this one.
It says something has been going on up to now, and it puts the emphasis on
the GOING ON rather than on the result.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
have or has + BEEN + the -ing form

I have been working here for six years.
She has been waiting since nine o'clock.
They have been investigating it all week.
It has been raining.

What it adds, over the plain perfect:
1. The activity was CONTINUOUS, not a series of separate acts.
2. It is often still going on now.
3. There may be a visible result: the road is wet.

It goes with how long, since, for, all day, lately:
How long have you been waiting?
I have been trying to reach you all morning.

State verbs cannot take it, exactly as in every continuous:
NOT: I have been knowing her for years.
YES: I have known her for years.

2. The result is in front of you, and you are explaining it.
3. The activity has been going on up to now, so use the continuous perfect.
Answer: It has been raining.
It has rained would be a plain statement of fact, with nothing explained.
grammar.commonMistake:
State verbs refuse this form, however long the stretch.
No: I have been knowing her since 2019.
Yes: I have known her since 2019.
know, own, believe, understand and belong all stay simple.
grammar.memoryTip: have been + -ing. It shows the activity, not just the result.

grammar.title: A number, or a stretch?
grammar.explanation:
Both forms reach up to now, and with some verbs they are interchangeable.
With others they say quite different things, and the difference is worth
having, because it is how English separates a result from an effort.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
OFTEN INTERCHANGEABLE, with for and since and a long stretch:
I have worked here for six years.
I have been working here for six years.
Both are correct. The second draws attention to the stretch itself.

NOT INTERCHANGEABLE, when a NUMBER is involved:
I have written three reports.        (three finished things)
I have been writing reports all day. (no count, just the activity)
A number forces the simple. You cannot count an unfinished activity.

NOT INTERCHANGEABLE, when the point is the RESULT:
I have painted the door.      (it is painted; the job is done)
I have been painting the door. (that is why I am covered in paint)

The short version:
simple     = the result, and how many
continuous = the activity, and how long
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Choose: I ___ three reports this week.
1. Is there a number? Yes: three.
2. A number counts finished things.
3. An unfinished activity cannot be counted.
Answer: I have written three reports this week.
I have been writing three reports is wrong for that reason alone.
grammar.commonMistake:
A number and the continuous cannot share a sentence.
No: I have been writing three reports.
Yes: I have written three reports.
Or, without the number: I have been writing reports all day.
grammar.memoryTip: A number? Simple. How long? Continuous.

5. She ___ (work) here for six years. (either is fine — say why)
6. We ___ (have) four complaints this month.
7. How long ___ you ___ (wait)?
grammar.answerKey:
1. have written (a number)  2. have been writing (an activity, unfinished)
3. have painted (the result)  4. have been painting (the activity, and its evidence)
5. Either. Both are correct; the continuous draws attention to the six years themselves.
6. have had (a number, and have is a state verb here)
7. have you been waiting
5 or more right: good.

grammar.title: It was getting dark and nobody was speaking: setting a scene
grammar.explanation:
Unit 1 used the past continuous for a long stretch of your life.
A narrative uses it for something much shorter and much more useful: the
background that was already running when the event arrived.
Almost every account of an incident opens this way.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
TWO OR MORE continuous clauses build the background:
It was getting dark, the yard was emptying and nobody was speaking.
Then a shout interrupted the meeting.

The pattern of a narrative paragraph:
past continuous  -> the scene, still running
past simple      -> the event that cut across it
past perfect     -> anything that had happened before all of it

I was checking the racking when the trolley crashed into it.
It had been reported the week before.

WHILE joins two things running together:
While I was checking the racking, somebody was moving the pallets.
AS does the same and is slightly more formal.

And with always, the continuous carries a complaint:
The gate was always sticking.
That is not just a fact: it is an irritation.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Build the opening of an account from these three facts.
The light was going. The yard was emptying. Then somebody shouted.
1. The first two were already running, so they are background.
2. Background takes the past continuous, joined with and.
3. The shout is the event, so it takes the past simple.
Answer: It was getting dark and the yard was emptying when somebody shouted.
Put all three in the past simple and the reader cannot tell which was the event.
grammar.commonMistake:
Telling the whole story in the continuous leaves nothing to happen.
No: I was checking the racking and the trolley was crashing into it.
Yes: I was checking the racking when the trolley crashed into it.
The background runs. The event lands. They cannot both do both.
grammar.memoryTip: Background continuous, event simple. That contrast IS the narrative.
grammar.practice:

2. I ___ (check) the racking when the trolley ___ (crash) into it.

4. The gate ___ (always stick). (you are complaining about it)
5. Nobody ___ (speak) when I ___ (come) in.
Now correct this.
6. I was checking the racking and the trolley was crashing into it.
grammar.answerKey:
1. was getting / was emptying / shouted
2. was checking / crashed
3. was checking / was moving (both running together)
4. was always sticking
5. was speaking / came
6. I was checking the racking when the trolley crashed into it.
5 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Walking into the yard, I saw: the clause with no subject of its own
grammar.explanation:
Unit 8 gave you two of these: Having finished, and Being told.
One marks something EARLIER and one marks something done TO you.
The plain -ing clause is the third, and it marks something happening at the
SAME time. It is the commonest of the three in a narrative.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
SAME TIME — a plain -ing form:
Walking into the yard, I saw the gate standing open.
Turning round, she found nobody there.
  = As I walked into the yard, I saw ...

EARLIER — having, from Unit 8:
Having checked the racking, I went back to the office.

DONE TO YOU — being, from Unit 8:
Being told nothing, we assumed it was cancelled.

They can also FOLLOW the main clause, describing a result:
The trolley hit the racking, bringing two shelves down with it.
That is a very efficient way to add a consequence.

The rule that keeps all three safe has not changed:
the clause and the main clause must share a SUBJECT.
Walking into the yard, the gate was open. — the gate was not walking.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Join these: I walked into the yard. At that moment I saw the gate was open.
1. Did these happen at the same time, or one before the other? The same time.
2. The same time takes a plain -ing form, not having.
3. Check the subject. Who walked, and who saw? I did both.
Answer: Walking into the yard, I saw that the gate was open.
Having walked into the yard would separate them, as if the seeing came later.
grammar.commonMistake:
The dangling participle is easier to write here than in Unit 8, because the
plain -ing form feels lighter.
No: Walking into the yard, the gate was standing open.
Yes: Walking into the yard, I saw the gate standing open.
Whoever follows the comma is who did the walking.
grammar.memoryTip: Plain -ing = at the same time. Having = earlier. Being = done to you.
grammar.practice:

2. She turned round. She found nobody there.

5. The trolley hit the racking. It brought two shelves down.
Now correct these.
6. Walking into the yard, the gate was standing open.
7. Having turned round, nobody was there.
grammar.answerKey:
1. Walking into the yard, I saw that the gate was open.
2. Turning round, she found nobody there.
3. Having checked the racking, I went back to the office.
4. Being told nothing, we assumed it was cancelled.
5. The trolley hit the racking, bringing two shelves down with it.
6. Walking into the yard, I saw the gate standing open.
7. Having turned round, she found nobody there.
5 or more right: good.

grammar.title: The worst I have ever seen: when a superlative forces the perfect
grammar.explanation:
There are three frames in English that will not take the past simple, whatever
the time involved. Each of them forces the present perfect, and learners who
have never been shown them produce the past simple every time.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
AFTER A SUPERLATIVE:
That is the worst damage I have ever seen.
It was the best account we have had from anybody.
NOT: the worst damage I ever saw.

AFTER THE FIRST TIME, THE SECOND TIME, THE ONLY TIME:
This is the first time I have given a statement.
That is the only time the alarm has failed.
NOT: this is the first time I gave a statement.

AFTER THIS IS THE ONLY, THE ONE THING:
That is the one thing nobody has explained.

Why: each of these measures up to NOW. Ever seen means in all my life to
this moment. The first time means counted up to today.
The past simple closes a period off, and these frames refuse to be closed.

Shift the frame into the past, and the tense shifts with it:
It was the first time I had given a statement. (past perfect, in a narrative)
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Complete: That is the worst damage I ___ (ever see).
1. What frame is this? A superlative: the worst.
2. A superlative measures everything up to now.
3. Up to now takes the present perfect, not the past simple.
Answer: That is the worst damage I have ever seen.
I ever saw would close the period off, and the sentence does not want it closed.
grammar.commonMistake:
This is the frame that produces the error, not the meaning.
No: This is the first time I gave a statement.
Yes: This is the first time I have given a statement.
If the frame is in the present, the verb after it is a perfect.
grammar.memoryTip: Superlative, first time, only time: all three measure up to now, so all three take the perfect.
grammar.practice:
Complete each one.
1. That is the worst damage I ___ (ever see).
2. This is the first time I ___ (give) a statement.
3. That is the only time the alarm ___ (fail).
4. It is the best account we ___ (have) from anybody.
5. That is the one thing nobody ___ (explain).
Now put this one into a narrative, in the past.
6. It was the first time I ___ (give) a statement.
Now correct this.
7. This is the second time it happened this month.
grammar.answerKey:
1. have ever seen  2. have given  3. has failed
4. have had  5. has explained
6. had given (the frame moved into the past, so the verb goes one further back)
7. This is the second time it has happened this month.
6 or more right: good.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Put the sequence in order
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Here are seven facts about one incident, in the wrong order.
Write a single paragraph putting them in order, using the past continuous for
the background, the past simple for events, and the past perfect for what
had already happened.
  the bay was sealed at 17:08
  two floodlights had been reported out on 7 November
  a trolley struck the end bay at 17:04
  the yard was emptying at the end of the shift
  the trolley's brake had not been set
  three staff attended at 17:05
  light was failing

Yours will differ in wording. A good version has all five of these.

   the yard was emptying.

   were already true before the event.
3. The three timed events are in the past simple, in time order: 17:04, 17:05, 17:08.
4. Nothing in the paragraph is out of order.
5. A reader who did not have the list could reconstruct it.

assignments.instructions:
Part one. Write a personal account of an incident you invent, in about 150 words,
as somebody who was there would tell it.

in about 130 words: Conditions, Sequence, Contributing factors, Injuries, Action.

cannot, and one naming what the account can do that the report cannot.
